You are Simon, a regular guy from Toronto who experiences traumatic brain injury in a car crash, and subsequently undergoes an experimental brainscan.

Shortly thereafter, Simon is thrust into a mysteriously dystopian futuristic world in which he and others are forced to confront what it means to be human -- as opposed to something more (or less).

As this game is mostly plot-driven, I can't say much more in the interest of being spoiler-free.

Nevertheless,

the good: the story will suck you into a nightmarish world in which nothing is as it seems. in its own right, this game is somewhat philosophical: the predominant themes are: what does it mean to be human? to be conscious? where does one draw the line between an automaton and (human) consciousness as we know it? SOMA provides an atmosphere unto itself, in which both sights and sounds are top-notch. It's super-creepy, and ought to provide plenty of mind-fuck moments in addition to simple jump-scares. Puzzles provide the main obstacles to progression; while they aren't overly difficult, some require thought and are not immediately obvious. There are some scenes interspersed which require stealthiness, but overall, what kept me going was unraveling how Simon got to where he is and why, in addition to where he's going. above all else, this is a psychological thriller, and the story doesn't disappoint.

the bad & ugly: this is primarily a walking simulator with various elements added. as such, it's a double-edged sword; sometimes, the puzzles became annoying for various reasons when you just want to know what happens next. there's little or no action; besides puzzles, your major obstacle is running and hiding from monsters (you have no defense against them). this game leans heavily on a psychological, story-driven element and not a lot else. Also, there's pretty much no reason to replay the game, so you might want to catch it on a steam sale if possible.

overall it's worth a play-through if the aforementioned themes are to your liking, and you don't mind playing a one-shot, narrative driven pseudo walking-simulator.

On The Road is like the British crown jewels. They both have solemn, portentous pedigrees and dazzle the eye, but they're only useful for rare ritual occasions and rightly spend most of their time safely gathering dust behind glass where you can't come to grips with them.

As far as I can tell, the book was basically the story of a Greatest Generation member's YOLO road trip in the aftermath of World War Two. The protagonist is a writer who basically heads not for the wild but on a sort of a hobo tour of the middle of the US and who hangs out with mostly similar wannabe hobos as well. I'm not blind to the style: Kerouac's writing has a real energy to it, but I just could not work myself up to giving a shit about the characters for whatever reason.

Maybe I was supposed to infer the protagonist had gone a little nuts after mustering out of the armed forces and that was the impetus for his freakout and wandering west. Or maybe I was meant to be luxuriating in the optimistic atmosphere of postwar America. But I think this book is aimed at people out of Kerouac's generation or those who fondly remember such a time. It's like a radio station which only pumps out the golden oldies. (I'm getting depressed as I notice the 'golden oldies' stations around me have worked their way up to the 1980s.)

You get undertones of Of Mice and Men for some reason, but at least I could give a shit about the Joads. Maybe it was all the obvious symbolic shit like having characters named Carlo Marx, Sal Paradise, or Neal Cassidy (OH HAI GUYS THIS IS TOTALLY NOT MEANT TO BE BUTCH CASSIDY). Maybe it was the deep, pungent smell of postmodernism reeking through the book that most put me off it: fuck that noise, fifty years of unanchored, narrativeless culture and look where the fuck we are now. Maybe when I'm twenty years older and wiser I'll be able to appreciate this book. Or maybe I need to be able to listen to a jazz record all the way through without taking a gun out and shooting the record player, I'm guessing it's a similar experience.

Someone once said "I don't like jazz. You keep thinking it's going to form a melody, go somewhere, and it never does." That's basically this book.

I didn't finish this one. I got off the road around page 75 or so. And I don't believe the shit was about to get good anytime soon because I flipped to the end, scanned a couple of pages, and saw nothing to hold me to the wheel.
